result.summary: Cadmus, unaware that his daughter and grandson have become sea deities, flees Thebes with his wife and reaches Illyria. There he wonders whether the dragon he killed was sacred and prays to become a serpent, and he is transformed. His wife begs to share his fate, and both become gentle serpents who slip into a grove.

scenes.title: Cadmus flees Thebes
scenes.summary: Worn down by misfortune and omens, Cadmus leaves Thebes with his wife and wanders until he reaches Illyria.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus is losing his home and peace to a run of family disasters.

scenes.title: Cadmus and wife become serpents
scenes.summary: Cadmus wonders if the dragon he killed was sacred and prays to become a serpent. He changes, and his wife begs the gods to change her too. They become two gentle serpents and enter a grove.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus loses his human form and his power of speech, and the couple face parting.

characters.name: Cadmus
characters.description: founder of Thebes, exiled and turned into a serpent

characters.name: Hermione
characters.description: wife of Cadmus, who goes into exile with him

notable_quotes.reason: Cadmus's pathetic plea to touch him while he is still partly human.
Closing image of the gentle serpents remembering their human past.

analysis.text: Cadmus reads his suffering as divine vengeance for killing the sacred dragon, and he chooses the shape of his offence. Transformation here is both punishment and a mournful release.
Illyria was linked in Greek tradition with Cadmus and Harmonia, who were said to rule there and give the region its royal line.

legacy.text: The tale of the aged couple turned into serpents inspired later artists and poets, and Cadmus's transformation is often cited as a model of metamorphosis in literature.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's transformation is gradual and described bodily, with scales, a divided tongue and fused legs, showing his taste for detailed physical change.

language_notes.text: Cadmus's daughter Ino and her grandson Melicerta (Portion of the earlier fable) became the sea deities Leucothoë and Palaemon; Cadmus does not yet know.
Refers to the dragon of Mars that Cadmus killed at the spring; he sowed its teeth, and armed men (the Sparti) sprang up.
"Unerring resentment" means the gods' anger never misses its target; he wishes to become a serpent himself, as fit punishment.
"Thy" and "thyself" are old singular forms of "your" and "yourself"; "ye" in sentence 12 is the plural "you".
"Covert" means a sheltered place, here a thicket or hidden spot in the grove.

context_notes.text: Cadmus, founder of Thebes, came from Sidon; his wife is Hermione (Harmonia in other tellings). Illyria lay on the Adriatic coast.
The "prodigies" are ominous events, such as the deaths and madness that struck Cadmus's descendants at Thebes.

literary_notes.text: Cadmus flees as if the place, not he, were cursed, suggesting misfortune follows him; the narrator hints his flight cannot solve the problem.
His plea to touch him while he is still a hand and partly human stirs pity by dwelling on the fading humanity.
Hissing replacing speech shows the loss of human identity; he can no longer voice grief, only animal sound.
The serpents are gentle and remember their human past, softening the punishment and reversing the dragon's earlier violence.
